name: Haman
bio:
Haman the Agagite, son of Hammedatha, was promoted by King Ahasuerus above all the other officials, and all the king's servants bowed to him except Mordecai, who refused as a Jew. Enraged, Haman resolved not merely to punish Mordecai but to destroy all the Jews throughout the empire. After casting lots to fix a date, he told the king that this scattered people disobeyed royal law and offered ten thousand talents of silver to fund their destruction; Ahasuerus gave him his signet ring and full authority. Haman had letters sent to every province in the king's name, ordering the annihilation of every Jew, young and old, on the thirteenth day of Adar, while he and the king celebrated and the city of Susa was thrown into distress (Esther 3:1-15). His downfall, engineered through Esther and Mordecai, is told in detail in the chapters ahead. Invited to Esther's banquet and promised a second the next day, Haman left elated, but his joy soured when he saw Mordecai refuse to rise for him at the king's gate. His wife Zeresh and his friends advised him to build a gallows fifty cubits high and ask the king the next day to hang Mordecai on it; pleased, Haman had it built (Esther 5:9-14).

 That same night, Haman came to the palace intending to ask the sleepless king's permission to hang Mordecai, but Ahasuerus instead asked him how to honor a man he delighted in; assuming the king meant himself, Haman proposed royal robes, the king's horse, and a city procession — only to be ordered to give Mordecai exactly that honor himself. Haman led his enemy through the streets proclaiming his honor, then went home in humiliated mourning, where his wife Zeresh and advisors warned he could not prevail against Mordecai. Before he could recover, the king's chamberlains hurried him off to Esther's second banquet (Esther 6:1-14). At Esther's second banquet, she finally named him as the enemy plotting to destroy her and her people; the king, enraged, stepped out to the garden, and on his return found Haman fallen on the queen's couch pleading for his life, which he took as an assault. Harbonah the chamberlain then pointed out the very gallows Haman had built for Mordecai, and the king had Haman hanged on it (Esther 7:1-10).
